results.title: Nebius Is Raising the Price of Its AI Compute on Oct. 1. Here's What That Says About the Shortage. | The Motley Fool
highlights:
## Key Points

- Nebius' on-demand hourly rates for four Nvidia GPU models climb between 17% and 21% on Oct. 1.
- Management says it could sell all its 2027 capacity today on the terms of its newest contracts.
- The company expects to spend $20 billion to $25 billion on capital expenditures this year.

Nebius Group (NBIS -9.92%) is about to charge more for the computing power it rents out by the hour. On Thursday, Oct. 1, the artificial intelligence (AI) cloud company's on-demand rate for an Nvidia B300 graphics processing unit (GPU) climbs 21%, from $7.85 per hour to $9.50.

Nebius expects to spend $20 billion to $25 billion on capital expenditures this year, versus guided revenue of $3 billion to $3.4 billion. A company building capacity so fast normally needs to work to fill it, not raise prices on it.

...

The Oct. 1 increase isn't the first this year. In early May, Nebius' pricing page showed the older H100 chip at $2.95 per hour and the B300 at $6.10.

After this round, the same chips will cost $4.50 and $9.50 -- around 53% and 56% more than five months before. This round includes four Nvidia GPUs (the H100, H200, B200, and B300), with hikes of 17% to 21%, plus Nebius' CPU-only servers.

...

"[W]e sold out of capacity because, as fast as we bring capacity online, we can sell it," CFO Dado Alonso said on the company's second-quarter earnings call in August.

CEO Arkady Volozh went further in the shareholder letter, saying Nebius could sell all its 2027 capacity today on the terms of its newest deals. It's saving some for customers with immediate needs instead. What's more, its first capacity auction cleared at the highest price Nebius has seen for Nvidia's Blackwell chips, 15% over anything it had charged earlier.

...

Less than the new rates could suggest. Nebius sells computing power both by the hour and under reserved-capacity contracts, but it doesn't break out how much revenue comes from each.

Still, at the end of June, Nebius had around $37.5 billion in remaining performance obligations (signed contract revenue it hasn't recognized yet), over 60 times its second-quarter revenue of $582 million. And these contracts are priced when they're signed, so an Oct. 1 increase doesn't reprice them.

...

Of course, shortage pricing can reverse. If supply catches up to demand while Nebius and its rivals keep building, hourly rates might drop as fast as they rose. And the build-out is being funded partly by $5.75 billion in convertible notes sold in August and around $2.8 billion in new shares sold through June.

results.title: Nebius raises Nvidia GPU rental rates up to 21% effective October 1, led by B300 at $9.50/hr · AI Factor News
highlights:
# Nebius raises Nvidia GPU rental rates up to 21% effective October 1, led by B300 at $9.50/hr

...

A supplier raising prices into record capex is the strongest possible signal that AI compute demand still exceeds supply — including for last-gen H100s, up 53% since May. It is bullish for the entire AI infrastructure revenue chain (Nvidia's pricing power, Micron's memory pricing power, datacenter landlords), and it is pure pricing power for neoclouds. The bearish offset is real: it raises the cost floor for AI startups' unit economics, which is exactly why falling inference costs matter to the thesis — someone has to make the math work for the renters. For the overbuild debate, this is bear-case kryptonite in price form: overbuilt markets cut prices; this market raises them.

## Summary Nebius raised on-demand AI compute pricing 17-21% across H100/H200/B200/B300 effective October 1, with the B300 going from $7.85 to $9.50/hour — into a year when it is spending $20-25B in capex on $3-3.4B guided revenue.

results.title: Something doesn't add up in AI inference economics. | Chris Nicol
highlights:
Last week, Nebius announced price increases of 17-21% across H100, H200, B200 and B300 GPU capacity effective October 1. You can see the updated pricing on their website.

At first glance, that seems completely reasonable. Demand for AI infrastructure remains strong.

But there's something curious happening at the same time.

While GPU rental pricing is increasing:
• Market price of inference continues to fall.
• Open models are getting better.
• Model providers are competing aggressively.
• API pricing is becoming increasingly transparent.
• Customers can compare token prices almost instantly.

In a typical technology market, new generations of hardware tend to push the cost of previous generations lower.

Instead, we're seeing a situation where the cost of compute remains firm, while the revenue generated by that compute faces continuous pricing pressure.

results.title: GPU spot et instances interruptibles : prix et risques
highlights:
La réponse courte : une instance GPU spot ou interruptible coûte en général moitié moins cher, et jusqu’à 90 % de moins chez les grands clouds, contre la possibilité d’être reprise sans prévenir ou presque. Le préavis va de zéro seconde chez Google Cloud à une heure chez Novita, en passant par deux minutes chez AWS. C’est une excellente affaire pour les travaux qui sauvegardent leur progression et peuvent reprendre, et une très mauvaise pour un service en ligne ou un entraînement sans point de reprise. Parmi les leviers pour maîtriser la facture GPU, c’est le plus puissant et le plus risqué.

...

> Pour qui : un développeur qui veut un prix bas sans risque d’interruption, pour un travail qui ne sauvegarde pas sa progression.
> 
> À partir de : 0,34 $ de l’heure pour une RTX 4090 en Community Cloud, à la demande et non interruptible, facturée à la seconde.
> 
> Pour démarrer : ouvrir un compte Runpod et lancer le pod en Community Cloud ; réserver le spot aux travaux qui reprennent seuls.

## GPU spot : la remise et le préavis, fournisseur par fournisseur

| Fournisseur | Remise annoncée | Préavis avant interruption | Ce que devient la machine |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AWS | jusqu’à 90 % | 2 minutes, sans garantie | arrêtée, supprimée ou mise en veille selon la configuration |
| Google Cloud | jusqu’à 91 %, GPU compris | 0 seconde par défaut, 120 secondes en option (préversion) | arrêtée en 30 secondes au plus, sans engagement de disponibilité |
| Azure | jusqu’à 90 % | 30 secondes, sans garantie | libérée par défaut, ou supprimée |
| Vast.ai | 50 à 80 % | non documenté | mise en pause, données conservées, reprise si l’enchère repasse devant |
| Novita AI | environ 50 % : RTX 4090 à 0,17 $ contre 0,33 $, H100 à 1,70 $ contre 3,39 $ | une heure de protection au lancement, puis une heure de préavis | reprise |
| Runpod | non affichée | sans préavis, selon son blog ; offre peut-être retirée | reprise |

Deux lignes méritent un commentaire. Google Cloud n’accorde par défaut aucun préavis : la machine s’arrête, et le délai de 30 secondes est celui qu’elle a pour s’éteindre proprement, pas celui qu’on a pour réagir. Novita, à l’inverse, garantit une heure pleine après le lancement puis une heure d’avertissement, ce qui transforme le spot en offre presque confortable pour des travaux de quelques heures. Chez Runpod, le statut des instances spot est devenu flou. Son blog prévient qu’elles peuvent être interrompues sans préavis, et sa page d’accueil les mentionne encore, mais elles ont disparu de la grille publique et de la documentation des pods, et un développeur rapportait le 27 septembre 2026 que l’API refusait désormais d’en créer. Mieux vaut les considérer comme indisponibles tant que Runpod ne les réaffiche pas.

Deux précisions valent pour les grands clouds. Le préavis de deux minutes d’AWS est donné « au mieux », sans garantie, et disparaît si l’instance est configurée pour se mettre en veille. Azure réserve ses machines spot aux abonnements payants : un compte d’essai ne peut pas en lancer. Dans tous les cas, le spot se prête mal aux premiers pas sur une plateforme, parce qu’une interruption inexpliquée ressemble à s’y méprendre à une erreur de configuration.

results.title: Why H100 Prices Are Climbing Again in 2026: Reading the Order Book Behind the 14% Increase — CheapestGPU
highlights:
H100 on-demand pricing is running about 14% higher year-over-year, with a market-wide median near $3.38/GPU-hr, even as Blackwell-class supply ramps. Demand has not moved at the same speed: reserved-term contracts signed before the ramp, driver/software maturity gaps on newer silicon, and procurement lag are keeping H100 capacity tight enough to hold price up. These are aggregated market numbers, not a CheapestGPU listings claim - the order book section below covers what is actually postable on this board.

...

Market-wide H100 on-demand pricing is up roughly 14% year-over-year and about 1.9% over the last four weeks, putting the median around $3.38/GPU-hr. That climb is happening at the same time B200 and other Blackwell-class supply is ramping, which on paper should pull H100 demand (and price) down, not up.

This is market-wide pricing context aggregated across clouds and marketplaces, not a figure pulled from CheapestGPU's own listings. CheapestGPU's current H100 inventory (`data/listingsIo.ts`) is three io.net rows, all SXM5, all reserved/term capacity at $2.20-$2.30/GPU-hr - not on-demand spot pricing, and not directly comparable to the on-demand market median above. Treat the two as separate signals: one describes the broader market, the other describes what is actually open on this board today.

...

A few forces keep H100 demand sticky even as Blackwell capacity shows up on order books:

- Software and driver maturity. CUDA, kernel, and framework support for newer Blackwell-class parts lags behind what is already battle-tested on Hopper. Teams running production training or inference pipelines are slow to re-validate a stack on new silicon.
- Reserved and term contracts already signed. A meaningful share of H100 capacity, including the rows on this board, is locked into 12 to 24-month reserved terms. That capacity cannot reprice or reallocate to Blackwell demand until the term rolls off, see B300 on the order book for how term length shapes what a row can actually do.
- Enterprise procurement lag. Budget cycles, vendor qualification, and capacity planning for large buyers move slower than the supply curve. A GPU generation can be generally available for months before enterprise demand actually shifts toward it.

Put together, Blackwell supply ramping does not immediately free up H100 demand, so the H100 price floor holds, or in this case climbs.

results.title: What it costs to rent an H100, B200 or RTX 4090 in September 2026: live prices from 28 GPU clouds — WPS
highlights:
GPU rental prices have not converged. The same card can cost several times more depending on which cloud you rent it from, and the cheapest option changes through the day. We run FastGPU, which pulls prices from 28 GPU clouds (marketplaces, neoclouds, serverless platforms and the hyperscalers) and ranks them cheapest first.

Here is the market as it stood on September 27, 2026 at 04:11 UTC, and the few patterns that decide whether you overpay. Prices move daily, so every figure links to its live page.

## The snapshot 

Cheapest on-demand price per GPU-hour for each card, next to the cheapest on-demand price for the same card at a hyperscaler (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud or Oracle). Every figure in a row comes from that card's live page.

| GPU | VRAM | Cheapest on-demand | Offered by | Cheapest hyperscaler | Gap (hyperscaler / cheapest) | Providers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 SXM | 80 GB | $1.79/hr | Cudo Compute | $5.38/hr (Google Cloud) | 5.38 / 1.79 = 3.0x | 22 |
| H200 | 141 GB | $2.60/hr | GMI Cloud | $7.91/hr (AWS) | 7.91 / 2.60 = 3.0x | 18 |
| B200 | 192 GB | $3.69/hr | DeepInfra | $11.28/hr (Google Cloud) | 11.28 / 3.69 = 3.1x | 16 |
| B300 | 288 GB | $4.89/hr | DeepInfra | $17.80/hr (AWS) | 17.80 / 4.89 = 3.6x | 12 |
| GB200 | 192 GB | $8.00/hr | GMI Cloud | $16.00/hr (Oracle Cloud) | 16.00 / 8.00 = 2.0x | 3 |
| A100 80GB | 80 GB | $0.89/hr | DeepInfra | $3.22/hr (Google Cloud) | 3.22 / 0.89 = 3.6x | 18 |
| L40S | 48 GB | $0.47/hr | Vast.ai | $1.86/hr (AWS) | 1.86 / 0.47 = 4.0x | 13 |
| MI300X | 192 GB | $1.71/hr | TensorWave | none listed | n/a | 4 |
| RTX PRO 6000 | 96 GB | $0.93/hr | Vast.ai | $0.97/hr (Google Cloud) | 0.97 / 0.93 = 1.0x | 11 |
| L4 | 24 GB | $0.11/hr | Vast.ai | $0.71/hr (Google Cloud) | 0.71 / 0.11 = 6.5x | 7 |
| RTX 4090 | 24 GB | $0.14/hr | Vast.ai | none listed | n/a | 4 |
| RTX 5090 | 32 GB | $0.21/hr | Vast.ai | none listed | n/a | 3 |

## 1. Hyperscalers charge 3.0x to 3.6x more for the same flagship silicon 

For the data-center flagships, the cheapest hyperscaler rate is 3.0x the floor on H100 SXM ($5.38/hr vs $1.79/hr), 3.1x on B200 ($11.28/hr vs $3.69/hr) and 3.6x on B300 ($17.80/hr vs $4.89/hr). The widest gap in the table is L4 at 0.71 / 0.11 = 6.5x. You pay the hyperscaler premium for the ecosystem (IAM, networking, managed services, committed-use discounts, startup credits), which can be worth it, but it is a choice rather than a default. The exception is the new workstation-class Blackwell card: an RTX PRO 6000 starts at $0.93/hr (Vast.ai) and costs $0.97/hr on Google Cloud, almost the same.

## 2. Spot capacity is cheaper again, with two catches 

If your job checkpoints, interruptible capacity cuts the price further: H100 SXM from $0.98/hr, H200 from $1.84/hr, B200 from $1.77/hr. The first catch: spot can be reclaimed at any moment, so it suits checkpointed training and offline batch jobs, never a user-facing endpoint. The second: the cheapest listings are often whole nodes. In the open dataset, the H200 spot floor on AWS requires 8 GPUs and the B200 spot floor on Google Cloud requires 8 GPUs, so the real entry ticket is that many times the per-GPU price.

...

## 5. The floor moves, so check it when you rent 

Marketplace prices change as hosts come and go, and a cheap listing can be rented out within the hour. Each GPU page carries a 30-day price strip showing the low, the typical price and whether now is a good moment to rent (for example H200 or L40S).

results.title: H100 Rental Price per Hour | Codelace
highlights:
An H100 costs about $2.89–$6.16 per GPU-hour across the on-demand examples below as of September 2026, with lower community and preemptible offers subject to different conditions. Runpod lists a single H100 PCIe pod at $2.89 per GPU-hour, while CoreWeave lists an 8-GPU HGX H100 node at $49.24 per node-hour, or $6.155 per GPU-hour when divided by 8. The rent H100 cost depends on form factor, node size, region, availability, commitment and what the bill includes.

## What is the H100 price per hour by provider?

The most useful comparison puts the required purchase unit beside each price. The table uses public provider pages opened on 27 September 2026. It excludes taxes, storage additions and data transfer unless the provider expressly includes them. A per-GPU equivalent for a full node is a calculation, not an offer to rent one GPU.

| Provider and product | Public rate | Required unit or condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runpod H100 PCIe, Secure Cloud | $2.89 per GPU-hour | Single GPU pod shown in catalog |
| Runpod H100 SXM, Secure Cloud | $3.49 per GPU-hour | Single GPU pod shown in catalog |
| Lambda H100 PCIe | $3.29 per GPU-hour | Single GPU instance |
| Lambda H100 SXM | $3.99–$4.29 per GPU-hour | $3.99 on an 8-GPU instance; $4.29 on a single GPU instance |
| Nebius HGX H100 | $3.85 per GPU-hour | On-demand rate shown before its announced October change |
| Crusoe HGX H100 | $3.90 per GPU-hour | On-demand GPU instance rate |
| CoreWeave HGX H100 | $49.24 per 8-GPU node-hour | $49.24 ÷ 8 = $6.155 per GPU-hour equivalent |
| AWS P5 Capacity Block | $37.76–$41.528 per 8-GPU node-hour | $4.720–$5.191 per accelerator-hour equivalent across listed regions |

The AWS row is a Capacity Block price for a scheduled reservation, so it is a different purchasing arrangement from unrestricted on-demand pods. The low endpoint appears on AWS’s listed regions outside its higher-priced US examples. A live marketplace can move faster than a fixed article. See the H100 price index and then confirm the machine and terms on the provider’s checkout page.

...

Single-GPU instances are easier to match to small experiments and inference jobs. Lambda’s public page lists its H100 SXM at $4.29 per GPU-hour for a single-GPU instance and $3.99 per GPU-hour within an 8-GPU instance. This is a clear example of a lower unit rate with a larger minimum purchase. At those posted rates, one hour of the 8-GPU Lambda instance costs 8 × $3.99 = $31.92, compared with $4.29 for the single-GPU instance. The larger node makes sense only if the workload can use its capacity or needs the connected topology.

...

Preemptible capacity can cost much less per hour, with the risk of interruption. Nebius shows HGX H100 spot capacity from $0.79 per GPU-hour versus its $3.85 on-demand rate. CoreWeave also lists a spot price for its full HGX H100 node; check the listed rate when booking. Google Cloud states that Spot VMs can be reclaimed at any time. Save checkpoints outside the temporary instance and include retry time in the budget.

Reserved pricing exchanges flexibility for a planned quantity and term. Nebius says large-scale clusters reserved for multiple months can cost up to 35% less than on-demand. Crusoe advertises reserved GPU resources through sales; its current public pricing page gives the H100 on-demand rate and asks buyers to contact sales for a reservation. AWS Capacity Blocks reserve specified GPU capacity for a scheduled window. A reservation may protect access to a machine, while a pricing commitment alone may only discount usage. AWS specifically says its Savings Plans do not reserve capacity.
